I was using a fizeau interferemeter to check out several cheap laser pointers a week or so ago.

The red laser showed fringes so I wanted to try making a hologram with it.

The beam, after expansion in a 40X microscope objective looked very wonky. I am curious what the pattern means and if I should even try using it to make a hologram.

Cheers.

posts.author: jrburns47
posts.content_md: From your brief description, it sounds like you’re not using a pinhole after the 40x objective. However, the photo looks a lot like a 40x in a spatial filter that’s been focused through a pinhole but hasn’t been fully tuned in on the z-axis… if not, then not adequate for good holograms.

know if this precluded holograms but said spacial filtering would help.

Cheers.

posts.author: Din
posts.content_md:
It looks a lot like Newton's rings (below). Usually a Fizeau is meant to test surface flatness, so it's possible that your geometry led to two surfaces in close contact, leading to Newton's rings. If these are Newton's rings, then it may be possible to make a hologram, albeit a thin hologram because of limited coherence length since your fringe contrast is not high. 

Try a Michelson since that is the best test of coherence. If you get fringes with equal path lengths, vary one path until the fringes disappear, and the difference is the coherence length. In this case you can make a hologram. If the Michelson fringes keep shifting suddenly then you have mode hopping and therefore multiple modes. In this case you can still make a hologram, but the hologram will have superimposed on it a series of diagonal lines across the image (what Colin Kaminski called "sliced bread")

![Newton's_rings_(650nm_red_laser_light).jpeg](https://holographyforum.org/forum/download/file.php?id=7866)
